summary: Defines DHCP options for finding the controller of the Broadcast and Multicast Service (BCMCS) in 3G cellular networks. A mobile node can be configured through DHCP to reach a particular controller, and the document defines the related options and codes. It is a standards-track memo.

eli5.summary: A phone needs to know which office to contact to receive a broadcast show. This memo gives a way for the network to tell it the office's address automatically.

subtitle: How a phone on a 3G network learns, via DHCP, where to find the controller for broadcast and multicast programs.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices using the Broadcast and Multicast Service (BCMCS) need the address of a BCMCS controller, and hard-coding it does not work when the device roams.
tldr.mechanism: Four new DHCP options carry the controller as either a list of domain names or a list of IP addresses, with separate DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 versions and rules for which one clients and servers prefer.
tldr.outcome: A device can ask DHCP for the controller instead of being configured by hand. Domain names are preferred over raw addresses, and the options are not integrity protected.

today: RFC 4280 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says the service was still being developed for 3G cellular networks at publication in 2005.

sections.title: Why DHCP Needs BCMCS Options
sections.content:
The Broadcast and Multicast Service (BCMCS) is being standardized in mobile wireless bodies such as 3GPP2, OMA and 3GPP. DHCP (RFC 2131 and RFC 3315) already hands out many non-address parameters, but no option existed for configuring a mobile device to use BCMCS.

A mobile node (MN) must know the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the BCMCS controller so it can download details about a broadcast or multicast program. In a roaming environment, setting that address statically is unrealistic. So DHCP is used to give the MN either the controller's IP address or its fully qualified domain name (FQDN).
sections.eli5: If you travel, you cannot memorize the phone number of every local TV office. So the network tells your phone the right number when you arrive.

sections.title: The 3GPP2 BCMCS Network
sections.content:
The RFC sketches the 3GPP2 model: an MN/user, a radio access network, a BCMCS content server, a BCMCS controller and a DHCP server. Only the MN and the DHCP server matter to this document.

The MN talks to the BCMCS controller to get program information such as scheduled time, multicast IP address and port numbers. The controller may also authenticate the MN while it fetches security information such as an encryption key. These interactions may happen over HTTP and XML as defined in the 3GPP2 specification. There may be more than one controller, so the MN should discover the appropriate one.
sections.eli5: The controller is like a TV guide desk: it tells your phone when a show is on and how to tune in. The network may have several desks, so the phone must find the right one.

sections.title: The Domain Name List Options
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 BCMCS Controller Domain Name List option uses code 88, followed by a length and the FQDNs. The option MAY contain several names, which SHOULD be used to build Service Record (SRV) lookups as specified in the 3GPP2 document, rather than querying for different A records. The list MAY include the access provider's own domain and those of partner networks, such as MVNOs (Mobile Virtual Network Operators). The RFC's example is an operator with two MVNOs, giving operator.com, mvno1.com and mvno2.com. If the client has no preferred name, it should use a default such as the first one in the list.

If the list is longer than the 254 octets allowed in one option, it MUST be encoded as described in RFC 3396. Names MUST be concatenated and encoded as in section 3.3 of RFC 1035, and DNS name compression MUST NOT be used.

The DHCPv6 version is OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_D (code 33). It has the same content and format as the DHCPv4 list, without the Code and Len fields, preceded by a 16-bit option code and a 16-bit option-length.
sections.eli5: The network gives the phone a short list of website-style names, such as the operator's and its partners'. The phone picks one it likes, or just the first.

sections.title: The Address Options
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 BCMCS Controller IPv4 Address option uses code 89. It carries a list of controller IPv4 addresses, which MUST be listed in order of preference. Its minimum length is 4 and the length MUST be a multiple of 4.

The DHCPv6 equivalent, OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_A (code 34), MUST carry one or more 128-bit IPv6 addresses of the BCMCS controller in an operator's network. Its option-length is the length of the address field in octets.
sections.eli5: Instead of a name, the network can hand over the street address directly, with the best choice first.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A DHCPv4 client MAY ask for either or both options in the Parameter Request List (code 55 from RFC 2132). A DHCPv6 client MAY use the Option Request Option (ORO) from RFC 3315.

If the client gets both a domain name list and an address option, it SHOULD use the domain name list. It SHOULD NOT use the address option unless the servers in the list cannot be resolved or reached.

A server MAY send either type if configured to do so. If asked for both and configured with both, it MAY send only one, in which case it SHOULD send the domain name list. If the client asked only for the address option and the server has addresses, the server MUST send it. If the client asks for one type and the server only has the other, the server MUST return what it has.

The RFC summarizes the server's response in a table keyed on what the client requested.
sections.eli5: The phone asks for a name or an address. The network tries to answer, and if it only has the other kind, it gives that. A name is the preferred answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no new security concerns beyond basic DHCP (RFC 2131) and DHCPv6 (RFC 3315). It does note that without message integrity protection for these options, an attacker could modify the option values to divert requests for broadcast service.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could change the note the network gives your phone and send you to the wrong desk.

sections.title: Assigned Option Codes
sections.content: IANA assigned four codes. The domain name list is 88 in the DHCPv4 option space and 33 (OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_D) in the DHCPv6 space. The IPv4 address option is 89 in DHCPv4, and the IPv6 address option is 34 (OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_A) in DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note gets its own number so everyone knows which one is which.
